abstract: Semelparity, - reproducing once in a lifetime - is an extreme solution to the trade-off between reproduction and future survival and is exceedingly rare in terrestrial vertebrates. Males of the Australian genera Antechinus, Phascogale and Dasykaluta are obligately semelparous while females are iteroparous, suggesting that the sexes face such different selective pressures that they have evolved different solutions to the same trade-off. Using invasion analyses of a novel two-sex population model with continuous reproductive investment, we show that the geometry of the reproduction-survival trade-off determines whether semelparity is evolutionarily accessible, but not necessarily whether it evolves. Age-structured survival and fecundity may maintain iteroparity under trade-off shapes for which classical theory predicts semelparity. Early onset of post-reproductive mortality can flip otherwise iteroparous trade-offs to semelparity, but only when survival declines quickly after sexual maturity. In contrast, when sexual competition gives high-investing males sufficiently disproportionate paternity, male-only semelparity can evolve under any trade-off geometry we examined, while females remain iteroparous. That male-only semelparity is rare while male competition is common suggests that lethal male investment evolves only under a particular combination of demographic, environmental and mating-system conditions.
